title: Superprestige Niel: Manon Bakker masters the mud to take the win
author: Owen Rogers
text:
Manon Bakker took her first Superrestige series win on Wednesday, the Velosport Veluwe rider dominating the race, riding alone to take the victory at the Jaarmarktcross in Niel.

Bakker escaped on the second of the five laps of the muddy course, eking out a lead and holding it. She eventually crossed the line 14 seconds ahead of Italian champion Sara Casasola (Crelan-Corendon) in second, with Denise Betsema (De Ceuster Bouwkranen) third.

The race was notable for the abandon of World Champion Lucinda Brand, the Baloise-Poetsbureau Lions rider crashing out on the opening lap.

With Bakker well ahead early on in the race, the day became a huge battle for the podium places, with Betsema edging clear first before Casasola launched her bid to close down Bakker late in the piece.

Bakker has had an excellent start to the year, opening her 2026/27 by winning six North American races from eight starts before returning to Europe for her first season riding as a privateer, running her own team.

In conditions which suited her to the ground, Bakker rode an almost flawless race, building her advantage quickly and defending brilliantly, slipping over only once, in the thick mud.

The third round of the season-long Superprestige series, the annual Jaarmarktcross in Niel, was held over five laps of a varied course, with plenty of sand, a series of what look like moguls, short sharp climbs, run-ups and plenty of mud.

The first sand pit came early in the lap, and, with none of the riders able to ride it, the bunch was spread in the first few hundred metres. Amandine Fouquenet (Pauwels Sauzen-Altez Industriebouw) exited in first place, and with teammate Leonie Bentveld behind her, the French rider quickly had a gap.

After winning the European title in controversial circumstances , Brand set off in pursuit. However, on one of the many short climbs she hit the barrier and was forced to retire from the race with an injury to her ankle.

As Brand rode back to her team camper, Fouquenet was caught, with Aniek van Alphen (777TV) and Bakker briefly gapping the two Pauwels Sauzen riders.

However, as the second lap wore on, the in-form Bakker, fresh from a clutch of race victories in North America, rode clear, taking a lead of 18 seconds into lap three ahead of an expanded six-woman chasing group.

At the end of the third lap, she had lost only one second of that advantage, with Betsema and Casasola beginning to eat away at the lead.

On the final lap, Casasola dropped Betsema and began to pressure Bakker, closing in, almost to within touching distance, but the Dutch rider held her nerve and form to take the win.

title: Diesel still costing close to a ‘dismal’ £2 a litre despite oil price falls
author: Zoe Wood
text:
Pump prices stay stubbornly high as leading bank official warns energy costs are likely to remain ‘elevated’

The price of diesel on UK forecourts remains stubbornly close to October’s record high of £2 despite a sharp fall in oil prices.

A litre costs an average of 197p, according to the AA, which described the situation as “dismal”. By contrast, petrol has fallen 6p to 168p from the peak of 174.7p in early October. That was the highest level since August 2022.

High fuel prices are putting huge financial strain on households and businesses and Christopher Waller, a US Federal Reserve governor, told a conference in London this week that energy prices could remain “elevated”.

He said a rise in tanker traffic through the strait of Hormuz came at a price: “The insurance now needed for ships making this passage, and the ship-to-ship transfer of oil necessary to guard against Iranian attacks, are reportedly boosting oil prices by $20 to $30 a barrel.”

Diesel production is also being affected by limited refining capacity and other constraints, Waller said, adding: “As a consequence, elevated prices for diesel in the United States are not expected to moderate as readily as crude oil prices would in a more peaceful Middle East.”

In the UK, the AA said that another 10p reduction could be on the cards for petrol because wholesale costs were falling. The wholesale cost of unleaded fell from 77p a litre to 68p in the second half of October, and now sits below 62p.

As a rule of thumb, each 5p reduction at the pump knocks £2.75 off the cost of filling a typical car’s 55-litre tank.

Luke Bosdet, the AA’s spokesperson on pump prices, said it was “hit and miss” but already possible to find petrol below 160p in certain areas, based on the government’s fuel finder data.

“London and the south-east stand out for not showing any fuel stations with the bargain petrol prices of northern England, Wales and even Scotland,” he said. “Some forecourts are still charging close to the peak prices of early October and, given how much wholesale costs have fallen since the middle of last month, that is unforgivable.”

The average diesel price is down only 2p a litre, from the all-time record of £2. With the wholesale cost down around 4p a litre since mid-October a further small reduction at the pump was possible, Bosdet said.

title: The One Metric Cyclists Over 40 Need to Start Watching
author: Josh Ross
text:
When I was in my 30s—not even my 20s—I could finish a hard ride, hydrate with a couple of beers, refuel with a pizza, and do it all again the next day. I didn’t think a ton about training in general because it was easy. If I wanted to ride faster, I rode more, and I got faster more or less no matter what I did. I even went through a long phase of severely underfueling; I weighed nothing, yet I continued to get faster. Then things changed.

The first place I really noticed it was when I transitioned from outdoor summer riding to indoor winter training. When that happens, I shift from endurance to intensity, and I used to just shrug it off. Surely if I could handle a six-hour outdoor ride on a Sunday, a three-hour indoor ride would be easier, no matter the intensity. Except my mid-week VO2 max workouts suddenly seemed awfully hard, and if I jumped into a Zwift race, it was all I could do just to hold on. Then that same three-hour ride the next Sunday felt awful. Pretty soon I almost dreaded getting on the bike, finding myself dragging to the saddle each evening for whatever workout I had.

The change was aging. One of the more fascinating things about testosterone as a performance-enhancing drug in endurance sports is that it isn’t just about building muscle. It works for performance because it allows you to recover faster and absorb more hard workouts. Guess what falls as you age? Both men and women experience hormonal changes as a result of aging, and reduced recovery capacity is just one side effect. There are plenty of other biological changes, and they all add up to a single reality: you have to start paying attention to a new metric you might never have considered before.

For younger riders, modern cycling technology—head units, smartwatches, and power meters—acts as an accelerator. It is a tool used to chase maximum power output, hunt Strava segments, and push deeper into the red. But to survive and thrive in your 40s, you have to flip that. To keep pinning on numbers and exploring remote gravel roads, your technology must become your brake.

Look, I’m a tech guy. I like “cool” technology and I had smartwatches pretty early on. At some point, I moved to Garmin watches primarily, but I continued to test Google Pixel watches, and for the Apple folks out there, Apple Watches have always been great options. Through most of that journey, though, I wasn’t doing much with those devices. Recovery metrics weren’t important to me because I tracked my on-the-bike performance with my bike computer.

I wore a smartwatch for occasionally tracking a run and because I enjoyed the smart capabilities. Who cares what happened off the bike? I’d ignore the advice to limit Zwift racing because it was fun. If I did three races in a week and sometimes saw my Garmin report that my HRV was unbalanced, I wouldn’t be concerned. But as I got older, I started noticing a pattern. On the days my Garmin told me my Heart Rate Variability (HRV) was unbalanced, my workouts felt terrible.

For a lot of people, HRV sounds very abstract. It also seems like something that just happens to you. In reality, it’s your body’s “check engine” light. It measures the microscopic variations in time between your heartbeats. A higher variation means your autonomic nervous system is relaxed, recovered, and ready to perform. A lower, suppressed variation means your nervous system is stressed—your body is fighting off lingering fatigue, poor sleep, or impending illness. Today, whether you are wearing a Garmin, an Apple Watch, or a Google Pixel Watch, they all track this baseline metric while you sleep.

When my HRV was unbalanced, it wasn’t just that the power targets were harder to hit. The bigger issue was that I didn’t want to ride my bike. Riding was always my favorite thing to do, but it was starting to feel like a chore. I’d struggle to motivate, and the slightest excuse became a great reason to do something else instead of whatever workout I had scheduled. If I decided to race anyway, I wouldn’t be able to really dig deep in the key moments, and I’d find myself not having much fun as I got dropped.

Then the even bigger problem was the downward spiral. In my 30s, pushing through was a badge of honor. In my 40s, pushing through a suppressed HRV just compounds the problem. Not only can you not perform your best, but the more you push through, the harder things get. You don’t ever have the capacity to recover.

I got to a point where I just thought, this can’t be life. Something has to be wrong if I feel like this. I even went and got checked out by my doctor, but the numbers were all within range. That was when I finally started to pay attention to the metrics I was getting from my smartwatch. Suddenly, HRV wasn’t something abstract; it was very real and very actionable.

That was the turning point. I had to learn to look at my recovery score, swallow my ego, and downgrade a hard interval day to a recovery spin—or take total rest. I learned it takes profound discipline to listen to an algorithm over my own ambition, but preventing that downward spiral is how older riders stay in the game.

In my 30s, my training plan was effectively nonexistent. If I had to sum it up, the strategy was simply: go hard all the time. Every sunny ride was about hunting for a PR, and I used to go on rides where all I did was mash up and down hills as fast as possible. There was a local hill someone bet me I couldn’t climb in under 20 minutes. I used to ride to the base with nothing held back, absolutely empty the tank up the climb, and then head home after a few minutes of breathing hard. I could shrug off anything.

You can get away with that “whatever, whenever, always hard” approach when your body naturally resets overnight. But as you age, it becomes a trap. Trying to hold onto that carefree adrenaline rush of racing whenever you want just isn’t sustainable.…

title: Records set by Toyota's WEC 2026 title-winning trio
‘I Expected More From Him’: A Lidl-Trek Teammate Says Out Loud What Many Were Thinking About Juan Ayuso
author: ahood
text:
Vacek, inset, watched as Ayuso struggled in 2026. (Photo: Getty Images)

Mathias Vacek might not be a household name yet, but he’s a rising star at budding super team Lidl-Trek .

And he clearly isn’t afraid to speak his mind.

In an interview with MARCA , the Czech rider offered a candid assessment of Juan Ayuso’s first season with the team, saying the Spanish star fell short of what he was expecting.

“To be honest, I expected more from him. He started good with the win in the Algarve, and it looked promising, but throughout the season I had the feeling something is missing,” Vacek told MARCA . “He was good, but not at the top like we were used to. I think everyone could see it.”

Ayuso moved to Lidl-Trek in 2026 after a blockbuster transfer and a controversial split with UAE Emirates-XRG. He wanted more freedom, and Lidl-Trek offered him a juicy contract and the chance to headline its grand tour ambitions.

After a hot start to beat Paul Seixas at the Volta ao Algarve , his spring came off the rails. He crashed out of Paris-Nice while in the leader’s jersey and then abandoned Itzulia Basque Country with illness.

Vacek, who made his Tour debut this summer, said he saw warning signs as the Tour approached .

“At the Sierra Nevada training camp, he had allergy problems, he went back home to Andorra, and he started training, but you could feel that something was going on. I don’t know whether it was mental or what,” Vacek said.

“I don’t want to say something I don’t know, but that’s my feeling,” he said. “In the end, at the Tour, you could see he was cooked, and Skjelmose was better than him. Definitely, for me when we signed him, I expected him to be like he was in the earlier years.”

Vacek was also quick to say that Ayuso can fly when everything clicks and stressed he was only sharing his observations, not criticizing his teammate.

“If he’s really good, if he’s on a wave, he can be top, he can also follow Pogi,” he said. “With these guys, when mentally something is wrong, if something wrong or a little detail is missing, they lose the confidence a bit.”

Vacek was equally honest about his own season.

The 24-year-old is emerging as a potential classics powerhouse , but his spring campaign fizzled. He didn’t hit the top 20 all spring and later saved his season with two stage wins and the GC at the ZLM Tour.

What happened? He says he overloaded too soon in an early season build in southern Spain.

“It was a season of ups and downs. Starting at the beginning, the classics went badly for me because I was tired. I started training quite early, and in Spain, with the good weather, you get into shape in three or four weeks,” Vacek told MARCA . “I got carried away with training so early. By the classics, when it really mattered, I was exhausted.”

A reset and an altitude camp helped turn things around. Vacek finished third overall at the Tour de Suisse, then completed his Tour debut by helping teammate Mads Pedersen secure the green jersey.

At the Tour de Suisse, simply staying close to Tadej Pogačar counted for more.

“When I was able to follow Pogačar on a stage of the Tour de Suisse. I think that was something even bigger than a victory for me, because there aren’t many riders capable of following him,” he said. “That was definitely the high point. And the worst moment, without doubt, was the crash in Montréal where I broke my nose.

“That’s cycling. There are always bad moments, but if you know you’re giving everything and committing 100 percent, you know the good moments will eventually come.”

Lidl-Trek brass clearly more upside and Vacek is signed through 2029.

Some see him taking over classics leadership from Pedersen when the big Dane retirees.

“Yes, I’ve had several one-on-one conversations with Mads. He’s a very honest person and tells you things exactly as he feels them,” Vacek told MARCA . “He has told me clearly that I’m one of the riders who will take over when he retires.”

Already four seasons in the WorldTour, Vacek says he’s not a carbon-copy of the marauding Dane, but admits he takes inspiration from the former world champion.

“I want to follow a clear path, try to be like him, and achieve the same victories. I’m a slightly different type of rider because I climb better, but I want to follow in his footsteps,” Vacek said.

“Everything I can learn from him now benefits me. I feel I’m gradually getting closer to his level, so I hope to be there soon if everything goes well.”

He’s obviously already taken one lesson to heart about being a leader — say what you think.

title: Pochettino a decade in Man Utd's making - but Carrick deserved better
text:
When the expected formalities of Michael Carrick's dismissal as Manchester United manager are completed after a summit meeting in Monaco, Mauricio Pochettino looks set to turn a decade-long courtship with Old Trafford into a full-blown relationship.

Pochettino and United go back a long way, with the Argentine's name associated with the club since he was spotted leaving a lunch appointment at Scott's restaurant in Mayfair with Sir Alex Ferguson in 2016.

Ferguson was three years into his retirement, while Pochettino was building his reputation at Tottenham , where he fashioned an intense, all-out-attacking team that the great Scot admired.

Pochettino called it "a meeting in London between colleagues, between a genius and an apprentice".

Pochettino was mentioned as a contender to succeed Louis van Gaal when he was sacked by United in May 2016, then when Jose Mourinho suffered the same fate in December 2018.

Pochettino was the other name on United's shortlist when Erik ten Hag was appointed in April 2022, then again when the Dutchman was shown the door in October 2024.

Finally, as Carrick awaits what looks to be the inevitable, it looks like Pochettino will inherit the Old Trafford empire.

The problem for Pochettino is that the once great footballing empire is crumbling before the eyes, the dysfunctional product of years of poor decision-making and questionable appointments, allied to a Frankenstein's monster of a squad assembled by six managers.

One of Pochettino's quirks is to have a box of lemons in his office, believing they absorb negative energy. He will need several truckloads of the industrial strength variety to suck away the current mood at Old Trafford.

First things first, however, and that means waiting for the official confirmation of Carrick's departure, a long drawn-out affair which does little credit to part-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe, chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox.

Carrick, 45, has proved to be out of his depth since being confirmed as permanent head coach following a successful interim spell, but his history of success as a player, his basic decency and his obvious desire to turn United's fortunes around makes the ham-fisted handling of his sacking another uncomfortable episode.

It is an emotion reflected by United's increasingly disaffected fanbase, who have made it clear who they blame for their current place in the Premier League relegation zone.

Pochettino ready to accept Man Utd offer to replace Carrick

The Monaco summit that will decide the future of Carrick and Man Utd

Would Pochettino be the right appointment to replace Carrick? Have your say

Pochettino's appointment would land in the middle ground between the flawed sentimentalism of turning to fan favourites with little or no track record of success, such as Carrick and Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, as well as the quick fix of bringing in proven past winners such as Van Gaal and Mourinho.

With his one-time dream of returning to Spurs now seemingly out of reach forever, Pochettino is ready to pick up the reins at the fallen giants that are United, another club he has clearly always had in his sights.

He is currently coach of the USA, whom he led at this summer's World Cup, but even then United were lurking on his agenda.

During the campaign Pochettino held court with invited journalists at the USA team hotel in California.

When mention was made of United, Pochettino turned to his closest confidante and ever-present assistant coach Jesus Perez to say: "One day, your dream comes true. You go to Manchester United ."

Perez replied with "United should have got you", promoting the response from a smiling Pochettino: "Future. Future."

The big question now is what Pochettino will United be getting?

He remains a beloved figure at Spurs , where he had an outstanding record of consistency following his appointment from Southampton in May 2014.

He never finished lower than fifth - in his first season - in any full campaign in charge, including second place behind Chelsea in 2016-17 and third in 2015-16 and 2017-18.

The one question mark always placed against Pochettino, including when he finished sixth at Chelsea in 2023-24, was an inability to get his teams over the line to tangible success in England.

Pochettino claimed the first trophies of his managerial career with Paris St-Germain after leaving Spurs - the 2021 French Cup and 2022 Ligue 1 title - but the club's hierarchy felt that was the minimum he should achieve given the squad at his disposal, and he did not see out his contract.

In England with Spurs , he was runner-up in the League Cup in 2014-15 and reached the FA Cup semi-finals in 2016-17 and 2017-18. In 2018-19 he reached the Champions League final and the League Cup semis.

In one season at Chelsea - a loveless relationship in which he could never shed his Spurs connections in the eyes of fans - he reached the FA Cup semi-finals and lost the League Cup final.

Pochettino's driven, competitive nature means that is an itch he will want to scratch when his United appointment is confirmed.

While Spurs have always appeared to be his first love, there is also no doubt United occupies a special place in his thoughts.

Spanish football expert Guillem Balague, who worked with Pochettino on his book Brave New World, says: "There is a fit with the people at the club too.

"Omar Berrada is a fan. When Manchester City drew up a shortlist to replace Pep Guardiola, some City supporters, including Omar, argued for Pochettino to be on it.

"There are plenty of clues about his feelings for United in the book. He was at the stadium in 1999 when United won the Champions League.

"Sir Alex Ferguson is mentioned 28 times, more than any other name in the biography.

" Spurs tried to push back and cut those references. Pochettino and I talked it over and decided that none of it would be touched. That shows how much it mattered to him."…

title: Cycling’s Lactate Superfuel Has Caused so Much Hype Riders are Sidestepping Sponsors to Get It
author: Jim Cotton
text:
Athletes are going off-sponsor to get lactate fuel. (Photo: Gruber Images)

Lactate fueling arrived with such wild hype at the Tour de France that it’s been forced undercover.

ExoLactate has launched an “unbadged” version of its revolutionary gels to meet a surge in demand from athletes who want to tap into the lactate boom, without causing a kerfuffle with team sponsors.

The pioneering Basque brand revealed its exclusive all-silver packaging on Instagram this weekend.

“ExoLactate Gel is used by elite-level athletes to fuel performance at the pinnacle of endurance sports. Sponsorship commitments mean many of these top-ranked ‘testers’ endorse ExoLactate anonymously,” reads the post .

“Now available is ExoLactate Classified, unbranded ExoLactate products, for elite application only.”

The launch of these secretive silver packets is a telling sign.

There’s some serious FOMO around what could be the next superfuel of elite endurance.

The secretive arrival of a first wave of lactate fuels at this summer’s Tour de Franc e was met with a swell of hype, intrigue and suspicion.

Exogenous lactate provides a third fuel source that works alongside the carbohydrates, glucose and fructose, and supercharges metabolism. We wrote a deeper explainer of how lactate fueling works, and why it’s not really “the enemy” here.

Insiders believe lactate fueling has the potential to be as big a breakthrough as the carbohydrate revolution or carbon-plated running super shoes.

But at present, the supply of these next-gen gels and drink mixes is limited.

ExoLactate and Enervit – the partner of Tadej Pogačar ‘s team UAE Emirates-XRG – are leading the boom.

Pogačar was guzzling Enervit’s lactate gel mix en route to his fifth Tour de France title this summer.

ExoLactate was supplying one of the Slovenian’s rival Tour teams, albeit under a strict anonymity clause.

ExoLactate and its “From Lab to Field” research group are also deeply embedded in professional trail running. The gels were used with wild success and podium results at the “Super Bowl” of ultra running, UTMB (Ultra-Trail du Mont Blanc).

Meanwhile, the rest of the carbohydrate-focused sport nutrition industry is scrambling to keep up with these lactate first-movers.

At present, only a small handful of derivative, scientifically dubious products are available.

But demand has skyrocketed since the summer.

Approval from Pogačar, proof-of-concept at the biggest bike and trail races in the world, and fear of missing out have made lactate gels a must-have.

ExoLactate founder Aitor Viribay told Velo that he experienced so much interest in his product – a gel that combines 5g lactate and 40g carbohydrate – that it was a no-brainer to launch “Classified.”

The anonymized packaging allows athletes to stray from sponsor commitments, undetected.

No taped-over gels or secretly decanted drink mixes necessary.

“We’ve had so many elites asking for a way to use lactate. And we wanted to support them because we believe in how much potential it has to change performance,” Viribay told Velo .

“But of course elites have their contracts with Maurten or Amacx or Science in Sport or whoever, and we respect that,” he said. “We don’t want to fight with those companies. But the athletes want to use lactate, and they are looking for ways to make it happen.”

Viribay – a former nutritionist at Ineos Grenadiers and the current head of performance at the Solomon running team – said the service honors ExoLactate’s two-way relationship with the elite.

The brand loses revenue and exposure through the service, but gains commitment, feedback, and trust in a fledgling product that’s still evolving.

“There was demand for the service from elites, so we opened the service,” Viribay said. “You have to apply and demonstrate that you have a commitment, and then we can sell to you with that unbranded packaging.

“We don’t make any more money selling the gels this way. These teams and athletes get special discounts,” Viribay continued. “But this is more a service for them because we want to work with them. We are born for elites. We are happy to help them because our goal is not just marketing.”

The professionalization and monetization of pro cycling means every nook and cranny of the sport, and the teams that compete within it, is sponsored.

In the past decades, team partnerships have exploded beyond bikes, helmets, and clothing to include nutrition, leisurewear, recovery products, and even bedding.

Contracts demand athletes “use” – or at least, are seen to be using – products from their team’s invested provider.

But in a sport where the margins are so fine, that’s not always what happens in practice.

Teams commonly ran blacked-out, off-sponsor wheels, saddles, and occasionally bike frames through the 2000s and 2010s. If something was faster, and a team could find a way to use it, they’d make it happen.

A more recent leveling in the bike-tech landscape has made this less of a “thing” in the Pogačar era.

However, off-sponsor pivots remain common in nutrition, where palatability and stomach-compatibility are unique to the individual and essential for success.

And in some cases, products are simply too good to miss.

Maurten’s carbohydrate hydrogels generated so much hype when they helped spark the carbohydrate revolution that the brand foreshadowed ExoLactate by selling unbranded products.

Close to a decade later, Maurten remains a top choice for the sporting elite.

Velo spoke to several WorldTour trainers and nutritionists who are skeptical of products that still lack published research and remain so novel in their use.

Viribay accepted the reluctance when he spoke to Velo . However, he was hopeful that the imminent publication of external studies will persuade the naysayers.

The Basque scientist also suggested the lactate curious more than match the skeptics.…

title: 'Increasing awareness between cyclists and motorists' – Garmin partners with navigation app Waze to increase rider safety with real-time alerts
author: Owen Rogers
text:
Bike tech company Garmin has announced a partnership with the user-based navigation app, Waze, to provide drivers using the app with real-time locations of riders.

It’s hoped the collaboration will increase rider safety, with drivers alerted to the presence of cyclists and better informed to slow down and take appropriate action. "By bringing Live Cycling Alerts to Waze, we’re giving drivers a helpful heads-up so they can slow down, stay aware and safely share the road," said Waze VP and GM, Gai Berkovich.

The system works when riders using one of Garmin’s compatible bike computers, like the new suite of Edge devices , or smartwatches activate the LiveTrack feature, using the Garmin Connect app on a smartphone. While this was created to allow riders the ability to share location, planned route and other features with family and friends, this now extends to the partnership with Waze.

"This collaboration brings greater peace of mind to cyclists by extending the benefit of LiveTrack to motorists using Waze for greater awareness of their surroundings," read the Garmin press release.

"Location sharing is temporary and session-based, and the cyclist’s personal information will not be shared or displayed in Waze." It also applies only to outdoor cycling activities.

Instead, what Waze users will see are 'Live Cycling Alerts' informing drivers of the cyclist’s presence on the road, with rider icons moving on the road in their vicinity.

"Garmin is well-known in the cycling industry for its safety-focused products and features, and we are excited to work with Waze to bring this unique feature to cyclists and drivers alike," said Garmin’s Vice President of Consumer Sales and Marketing, Susan Lyman.

"By increasing awareness between cyclists and motorists, this new tool is designed to foster a safer riding environment for Garmin customers by giving drivers valuable real-time visibility to their whereabouts, helping to create a more connected experience for everyone on the road."

Waze was created in 2009 as a community-based navigation application, which employs its users' generated travel information to provide the best navigation options.

title: What we know about worrying new Honda F1 reliability issue
author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
text:
Honda's worrying return of reliability problems includes a new issue, the root cause of which it might not trace before the end of the Formula 1 season.

Aston Martin and engine partner Honda suffered their third DNF of the triple-header in Brazil, when Lance Stroll retired for the second race in a row.

Stroll had two separate battery problems over the course of the Brazil weekend and didn't make it to mid-distance in Sunday's grand prix.

It means Stroll has finished just six of the 20 races held this season, while team-mate Fernando Alonso has had seven retirements of his own.

There have been some flashes of optimism - in relative terms, given how disastrous this first season of the new alliance has been - of late as Alonso scored points in Malaysia five races ago, had surprisingly good pace at Austin despite sustaining significant floor damage on the opening lap , and excelled in the wet in Brazil.

There, Alonso comfortably gave Aston Martin and Honda their best qualifying of the year, getting into Q3 for the first time and lining up eighth on the grid.

But this has been badly undercut by a return of significant fragility that's closer to how badly Honda started 2026.

Reliability problems also put paid to Alonso's chances in Mexico, where he had looked quite competitive and closer to the top 10 than normal. The issue was related to the cooling system inside the energy recovery system, whereas in Brazil the emergence of battery problems for Stroll sounded a clear alarm bell.

Shintaro Orihara, Honda's lead trackside engineer, acknowledged that "we know what happened, but we don't know what is the root cause".

He admitted it may take a few weeks to find that, but already from the data there needs to be some kind of countermeasure for the next race in Las Vegas, while Honda traces the underlying cause so it can be addressed properly for 2027.

"We need to find the actual root cause of this error for next year," he said.

"Otherwise, we keep having the same issue."

This was a different kind of failure to what had occurred in Mexico, which had led to MGU-K problems. But the theme is similar: in Mexico, Orihara had admitted to a lack of robustness within Honda's engine in more ways than one, and the fault there hadn't shown up in simulation.

Now Honda knows what happened but doesn't know why. That's a worrying through-line between the two issues. It also harks back to the start of the year, when Honda could identify the obvious catastrophic consequences of the problems that were emerging and could see broadly where they came from, but didn't know exactly what the problem's root was, because it had come out of the blue compared with what it had experienced on the dyno.

What's particularly alarming is that this does seem to be a regression from where Honda had got to in the middle of the season.

Its performance was obviously still lacking, and its engine is still underpowered on the internal combustion side, even with upgrades through the year to try to trim the deficit.

But it had at least got to a point where its cars were finishing races, which allowed Alonso to score some points when the Aston Martin was heavily upgraded.

Either side of the summer break, Alonso had five straight finishes, and Stroll got two of his six finishes this year in three races before the summer break too.

Orihara acknowledged that reliability was simply better in the middle of the season, but that has been replaced by "several issues" in recent races.

Some of this trend could be related to the mileage of parts - components simply coming to the end of their life cycle - or to just a case of Honda trying to run the engine harder for performance and going over the edge.

But with the battery issue that emerged in Brazil specifically, it's too early to say what the trigger was.

Honda has not made the progress it would have hoped for this season in terms of the all-round performance of the engine, and at best has only achieved some of its performance targets in very specific circumstances.

So the fact that reliability has got worse, without a clear upside, puts Honda under pressure and brings an unfortunate amount of negative scrutiny again, right at the end of a year in which it has had to come through quite a lot of adversity.

It is also a curveball for the development work Honda is doing on 2027, when it needs to take a step in both performance and reliability.

Everything that has been indicated so far is that there will not be a major step at the start of the new season. There's already a plan to phase in further upgrades through the year. But that work will already be deeply under way.

Troubleshooting takes away human resource, limited dyno hours which are restricted under F1's engine development limits, money that comes under the engine cost cap, and simply time because the clock is ticking to the start of 2027.

First the cooling issue in Mexico, whatever that was exactly, and now this on the battery side, takes Honda's focus away from a path that it would ideally be a lot further down.

Honda CEO Toshihiro Mibe was in Brazil, which Orihara said has a galvanising effect on the staff - "but on the other hand, we had a battery issue twice this weekend".

It was not exactly how Honda's F1 operation would have liked to present itself in front of the big boss. But, as Orihara noted, Mibe at least "knows what is happening trackside".

"He will bring this experience to the Japanese side and also boost our development," said Orihara.

If there was ever any possibility of complacency creeping in about how much work Honda has to do to reach the necessary standard, the CEO seeing first-hand the kind of problems still being encountered this deep into 2026 will have stamped it out.

title: 'I continued even after I thought it was fun' – Former U23 world champion retires aged 27
author: Patrick Fletcher
text:
Five years ago, Johan Price-Pejtersen looked to be on the verge of a highly successful career as a professional cyclist, but it is now fizzling out at the age of just 27.

The Danish rider claimed the U23 time trial world champion in Bruges in 2021, to go alongside his Danish and European titles. Beating Luke Plapp and Florian Vermeersch in Bruges, he announced himself as a future star and, though he did already have a professional contract with Uno-X, earned a move to the WorldTour with Bahrain Victorious.

After three years with that team, Price-Pejtesen spent the past two years with Alpecin-Premier Tech, but has decided to hang up his wheels at the end of 2026.

"It's an upheaval, but it's also a decision I made quite a long time ago," the 27-year-old said on the Danish Forhjulslir podcast.

"When you've been in cycling for a long time, you gain some experience. I've always said: 'I'll keep going until I don't think it's fun anymore'. Some things sound noble in the moment. The fact is that I continued riding my bike even after I thought it was fun."

As well as losing the passion for the sport, Price-Pejtersen also suggested he encountered physical problems that held him back.

"I had a period of two months where every time I went out to train, I felt like I had eaten something bad for breakfast, like I was going to throw up," he said.

"It's strange, but also true. I've spent some time thinking about it and getting used to it."

No pro win, controversially

Price-Pejtersen has raced sparingly since making his first and only Grand Tour appearance at this year's Giro d'Italia, where he placed a notable seventh in the time trial.

Since May he has only completed 10 race days, all on Danish soil, winding down his career with a final pro-level appearance at the Tour of Denmark followed by two criterium races.

Price-Pejtersen largely slotted into a domestique role over the years, and while he did achieve some strong results against the clock – including podiums at Tirreno-Adriatico and the Chrono des Nations – he never managed to win a race during his career.

title: 'We are certainly not doomed' – Thibau Nys and Lucinda Brand's cyclo-cross team in mid-season sponsor search after co-title sponsor pulls out
author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
text:
Sven Nys ' cyclo-cross team will be searching for a new title sponsor as Glowi, owner of cleaning agency Het Poetsbureau, is set to withdraw from its sponsorship deal at the end of this year.

Glowi took up a multi-year co-sponsorship of the team at the start of 2025, but the company had an option to withdraw at the end of each year.

"That option has now been exercised," Sven Nys, who runs the Baloise Verzekeringen-Het Poetsbureau Lions team, told Belgian newspaper .

The team currently have eight riders on their roster across the men's and women's elite and under-23 ranks, including recently-crowned European champions Thibau Nys and Lucinda Brand , and Annemarie Worst and Pim Ronhaar.

Thibau's father Sven said Glowi's decision to withdraw from sponsorship is unrelated to team results. reports that the company is facing its own difficulties.

"We built an incredibly good relationship with the people from Glowi and Het Poetsbureau, where I myself used to give cycling clinics to cleaning staff in all provinces. They were happy with our performance, and we gave them enormous visibility," Nys said.

"[The decision] is also completely unrelated to our team. They made a decision, and we respect it."

The team will continue with Baloise on board until the end of the 2027-28 cyclo-cross season, though they're now searching for a new co-title sponsor, with a contract set to begin mid-season.

"At a more difficult time for us than for a road team. Because we are in the middle of a cyclo-cross season and the contracts run until January 1. That leaves us in a tight spot," Nys said.

"In 2026, that applies to cycling in general and to every team looking for potential new partners. Unfortunately, in this sport, you are never all set.

"Companies that believe in us and 'want' to invest are our only income. It is a constant matter of keeping your feelers out. Discussions are ongoing. But you don't get something like this arranged in a few months."

Nys said that the team isn't in danger of disappearing from the cyclo-cross peloton this season.

He also denied that sports marketing and event company Golazo, which runs several cyclo-cross races and contributes to the team's youth structure and Sven Nys Academy, will step up to contribute to the senior squad.

"That is not true. We are part of 'the house', and they will of course continue to support us. But not in the way it is being suggested. No extra money will certainly need to be injected. In that respect, everything is covered for next year," he said.

"In the meantime, we have already found several additional shirt partners, who will be announced in the coming weeks. This means that we are already making concrete future plans.

"We are certainly not doomed. And we are diligently continuing our search... with the strong relationship with Golazo as a reliable foundation."

title: Pochettino’s Manchester United interest is as natural as it is disruptive to the US
author: Jeff Rueter
text:
The former Tottenham manager is always going to be a subject of interest, but United’s job carries a rare power

As Mauricio Pochettino left the podium to close his final press conference of the last international window, he offered an ambiguous farewell.

“See you next …” Pochettino began as he headed to the tunnels of Allianz Field in Saint Paul, before cutting his sentence short. Then, a bit of a sing-song: “See you next, see you next.”

You don’t need an AI clanker’s autocomplete function to try closing the sentence. “See you next month” would have been synonymous with “see you next window”, after all. Still, the farewell felt poignant given questions about whether Pochettino was going to last a full four-year cycle as US men’s national team head coach.

In hindsight, maybe he had omitted adding something along the lines of: see you next, before I’m off to my next project .

From the moment that Pochettino and US Soccer announced his contract renewal in August, it was tough for many to imagine he would don his lavish safari shirts on the US sideline at the 2030 World Cup. This was Mauricio Pochettino , after all, a name brand in club management whose résumé teemed with unfinished business. Few great coaches hang their hat on being Premier League and Champions League runners-up.

Gone are the days where clubs with major financial considerations pull the plug on a whim. The time to strike is now at the start of an international window, when the next game isn’t for another couple of weeks. This serves as a crucial time to meet the squad, put them through their paces and hatch an initial scheme to stop the rot.

That puts international federations like US Soccer in an unenviable position. Pochettino is among the most eligible options for the Big Clubs, ensuring his continuing presence on managerial wishlists. And as long as that remains the case, the most likely window for advances from club suitors will be right in the stretch of time where a national team coach works hardest.

In September, that meant reheating years-old discourses about the apparent irresistibility of Tottenham Hotspur . Before the World Cup, Milan had come calling . And now, the focus turns to Old Trafford.

The attraction is logical. For over a decade, United have tested every managerial archetype possible since Sir Alex Ferguson called time on his illustrious career. Domestic options who punched above their weight class; chronic winners; onetime supernovas, with implosion all but inevitable; club legends; club custodians; young options ready for a Premier League closeup. Their tenures all ended the same.

Pochettino blends some of the best traits of Louis van Gaal and José Mourinho with a record of doing the work United hoped would happen under Ruben Amorim and Michael Carrick. His work building Tottenham into a threat on all fronts bolstered his culture-building cachet, showing his success at Espanyol and Southampton could scale. Even though his time at Paris Saint-Germain failed to yield their long-coveted Champions League title, he had experienced managing the egos of Neymar, Mbappé and Messi. Chelsea tested his tolerance for ownership-meddling. All of these factors inform Manchester United at present.

So no, the idea of Pochettino leaving the US so soon into his second term is hardly a shock. If it wasn’t to be United, or Tottenham, then he’d be a hot commodity if Real Madrid were to quickly abandon their reunion with Mourinho. If not them, then perhaps Milan again if their campaign were to sour before the festive season. And so on.

US Soccer deserves some credit for adequately preparing. For one thing, Pochettino’s retention was only made possible thanks to a billionaire super-donor, Ken Griffin. So while his wages dwarfed those of his predecessors, it hadn’t directly come at the expense of the federation’s other teams, initiatives or grassroots efforts.

The real boon is his release clause, a reported $10m (£7.5m) option that only a Big Club could afford to spring. Had Pochettino left after the World Cup, coach and federation would have parted with nothing more exchanged than a handshake and some pleasantries. Instead, they forged an insurance policy to make up for what could have been if Pochettino had stayed for a full cycle.

Of course, piles of money don’t qualify for World Cups. Should this international window be Pochettino’s last with the US, the onus will be on the federation to do what it couldn’t this summer and find an alternative to lead a program into an exciting new era. It would be a boon to the federation if that $10m pot was kept on standby to help foot the next coach’s wages, keeping the pool of possible candidates open and deep.

US Soccer will need to nail the next hire to reassure fans who fell for the team during their entertaining run at this year’s World Cup. That will probably be a project-by-committee, as the federation hasn’t seemed antsy to replace Matt Crocker after he quit his role as sporting director in April. And, if Pochettino was unlikely to be in the role all the way until 2030, perhaps it is a blessing that a split comes while the cycle is still dawning.

title: What the Brazilian GP revealed about F1's ability to cope with rain
'I don't think I could do just one discipline' – How a mantra about circles, childhood friends and an unruly chicken help Puck Pieterse to do it all
author: Rosael Torres-Davis
text:
Puck Pieterse folds a slice of pizza the way New Yorkers do, and her very first slice was plain cheese, nothing else. She doesn't usually order it that way, she told me later; she just wanted to taste the basic version first.

That was lunch. For breakfast, she had a bagel with cream cheese and smoked salmon. Somewhere along the way, she hit the M&M's store in Times Square and went to town picking up every flavour she can't buy in the Netherlands. She ate enough that it made her feel sick. "It made me fly on the bike," she laughed. "I'm on holiday," she shrugged. Once her stomach settled, the leftovers became her post-ride recovery snack.

It was 24-year-old Pieterse's first time in New York, and she told a small crowd of fans that evening that it was a lot to take in: the noise, the lights, the sheer scale of it. "It's just so much bigger than my European mind can comprehend," she said.

She'd been to a Knicks game the night before. She was still processing the soundtrack: the organ, the sound effects narrating every possession, and an arena that left no doubt which side it was on, with ominous cues when the visitors had the ball and "crazy TikTok songs" when the Knicks did. You would never have guessed that from watching her ride on 8th Avenue at the start of rush hour earlier that day, or from how smoothly she handled clueless onlookers and city vehicles in a bustling Central Park just days before marathon weekend.

Later that evening, at Roberta's Pizza in Midtown Manhattan, I had a little over 20 minutes and three slices of cake to win her trust. We were both speaking our second language, and we were both frazzled by the room, but the sweets helped break the ice.

Pieterse rides for Fenix-Premier Tech , and everyone asks her the same question: how does she do it all? She races cyclo-cross in winter, the Classics in spring, and mountain bikes and the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift in summer, and she has won at the highest level in all three disciplines.

"It's definitely getting harder to combine everything because every discipline is getting way more specific," she told me. Her 2026 season showed the cost: podiums at Flanders, Flèche Wallonne and Liège-Bastogne-Liège, the Tour's polka-dot jersey and a third straight bronze at the cyclo-cross Worlds, but not the one standout victory she said she wanted.

The more interesting question is how she keeps her head clear while doing it, how a rider pulled in so many directions stays steady in each one. She came to New York between the road and CX seasons, for a community ride and pizza night hosted by Canyon and Zwift, and I spent the day trying to find out to that question. The answer, it turned out, involved circles. And not just riding around in them.

The question came from the crowd gathered on Roberta's rooftop, read aloud by the evening's host, Matt Stephens: did she have a mantra, or any trick for staying focused under pressure?

She has circles, Pieterse explained. Circle one is the race and only the race: your line, your effort, what you are doing right now. Circle two sits a little wider; it can be your mom or dad shouting from the tape, and they are allowed in briefly, but then you go back to circle one.

The danger is drifting further out. "On a bad day, you start hearing people talking about you, or your own head joins in with the negativity," she noted. She recognizes it happening and steps back inside.

Her race mornings are built to keep the first circle uncluttered. At a cyclo-cross race, her father prepares her pre-race meal, she rides two or three laps of the course, then tries to visualize it back at the camper, with Dutch rap in her headphones. Nothing superstitious, she insisted.

Back on 8th Avenue at peak time, circle one is a cab door, a delivery cyclist salmoning against the flow, a pedestrian stepping off the curb mid-text. Pieterse slid through the chaos without appearing to think. When I asked how she made urban survival look so effortless, she gave me a look that suggested it was not much of a question.

To her, it is simply second nature. "If you race a lot, you get a bit of awareness about what others are going to do, but of course you can never be one hundred per cent sure," she said. At home in the Netherlands, she rides through a city centre every day to reach her group ride meeting point. Dutch cities are smaller, she notes, but there are more of them, so traffic is woven into every training ride. She knows her routes, including – she admits with a grin – when she might sneak through a red light.

"I think if you're less into cycling and you're a tourist here, it's really dangerous actually with all the cars."

Still, she'd love to ride an alleycat race in New York, she said, before thinking better of it: it wouldn't be safe. NYC drivers, though, got a good review. "They know there are cyclists around, so that's nice."

I watched most of it from a few bike lengths back, on a Canyon Aeroad borrowed from her sponsor. I chased her through Midtown and into Central Park, where about 40 riders had turned out for the Canyon and Zwift community ride, on a loop already crowded with marathon-weekend runners and visitors. Over three laps, Pieterse found her way to the wheel of nearly every rider, chatting and making jokes as she went.

'Cross, Classics, and cake

Most fans on the ride wanted to know when her cyclo-cross season will start. Pieterse, who is still working out her 'cross schedule, was more curious about them: why they took up cycling in a city with so little room for it, and whether they only ride in the park or live somewhere with better roads. She was struck by how big the local community is, given how few bike shops she had spotted while walking around.

I'd heard Pieterse plans rides around bakery stops, so she didn't argue when I told her we would do a cake tasting while we talked. Cakes and sweets are part of the programme. At her local coffee stop back home, she orders apple pie in slices so massive they are meant to be shared.

She took the tasting seriously. The tiramisu was "surprisingly marshmallowy… when it should have been more mascarpone and alcohol," while the red velvet cake had the texture the tiramisu missed. "I know my cakes," she said. The key lime cake, airy and bright, ended up being her favourite.

Between bites, I asked how she manages to switch between disciplines. She splits her year into blocks: road, mountain bike, with the Tour de France sandwiched in between, then back to the mountain bike. 'Cross fills the winter, and by January, she is deep into the intense CX calendar. By the end of February, she has pivoted back to the road for the Classics.

The switch itself is smaller than people think, she insists. She trains on both bikes at home. She sees the Spring Classics and cross-country mountain biking as requiring the same type of explosive effort. The Classics are simply far longer, demanding deeper fatigue resistance.

The hard part is accepting what she has to give up. Her Classics rivals spend an entire winter preparing only for those races, while she is racing 'cross. Before mountain bike Worlds, she notes, she could have been at an altitude camp instead of racing the Tour.

"I'm fully committed to cycling and to becoming the best cyclist I can be," she said. She accepts the trade-offs because variety gives her so much. Pressed by the crowd that night to choose just one discipline or bike, she called herself an all-rounder, then picked the mountain bike. "For now," she added.

It circles back to her mental framework. The ground beneath her keeps changing, from mud to cobbles to singletrack, and her job is to keep circle one steady.

Her record explains why people keep asking about her ability to do it all. In 2024, she won the elite cross-country mountain bike world title, then a stage of the Tour de France Femmes on her first attempt, along with the young rider's white jersey. In 2025, she won La Flèche Wallonne , then five MTB World Cup races in a row.

Then came 2026. Before the Ardennes, she told her team she would "rather have one real stand-out result than three podiums." She got the podiums instead: third at Flanders, second at Flèche Wallonne and Liège-Bastogne-Liège, no win.

When asked which win she would relive, she chose the 2024 Tour stage from Valkenburg to Liège over the closing climbs of . That day, on rain-soaked roads, at just 22, she beat race leader Demi Vollering in a photo finish, with Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney third.

"I had, in the evening before, in the night, I woke up... I dreamed that I was winning today," she told the room. "And then in the end, the final, I just knew what was going to happen. It was super weird."

There is one major title still on her radar. She has stood on the elite cyclo-cross Worlds podium four years running, silver in 2023 and bronze in each of the three years since, but never on the top step. The next chance comes in Oostende, Belgium, at the end of January. A few moments after we talked about it, a stray balloon shaped like a number one drifted up over us and into the black-blue evening sky.

'It's sad that we don't have the US World Cups anymore'

Pieterse knows North American 'cross better than most Europeans. She won the under-23 world title in Fayetteville, Arkansas, in 2022, and has raced World Cups in Iowa and Wisconsin. No World Cup has come back since the 2023/24 season. The 2026/27 series has 12 rounds, including Glasgow on December 13, but none in North America.

When I told her that American cyclo-cross has struggled to regain its momentum in recent years, and asked what the US could learn from Europe, she was frank. "It's a very Belgian sport," she said. In Belgium, a fan can reach most races in about half an hour by car; here, she pointed out, it can take a seven-hour flight. What she liked about the American 'cross races she has done was the weekend format, with amateur and kids' races building to the World Cup on Sunday. She also wondered whether a late-season slot on the 'cross calendar might make the trip across the Atlantic easier on riders. Mountain biking, she noted, wrestles with the same question of where to put its World Cups.

"I think it's sad that we don't have the US World Cups anymore," she said. For riders, those races were a lot of fun, and though getting here is a long trip, "once you're here it's always been worth it." When the biggest names come, the public follows. Several people on the Central Park ride had told her they had watched her race 'cross here.

The other fix, she thinks, is online. "I think being present on social media can play a big role as well," she said, though geo-restrictions make races harder to watch in the US. And 'cross suits a screen: at "only fifty minutes to an hour," she said, a CX race is easier to watch than a mountain bike race.

Back to reality and racing

Whilst New York is something of a holiday, her next big trips away will be for racing. The 2027 Tour de France Femmes starts in Leeds on July 30, the race's first Grand Départ in the UK. She missed the big-name climbs of recent editions and sees chances for herself and Fenix-Premier Tech on a route with shorter climbs. "I think it will only make maybe even a more exciting Tour."

Home is Amersfoort, in the middle of the Netherlands, where she grew up and still lives. She started riding because her father came home muddy from weekend mountain bike rides with friends, and she wanted that too.

As a kid, she said, announcing she would turn pro was like saying "you wanted to be a police officer or a firefighter," something you say without really meaning it. Then, as a first-year junior, she had a good enough season to earn a spot at the Worlds in cyclo-cross and mountain biking. By the time she was under-23 and had signed with Alpecin-Deceuninck, she was suddenly sharing a roster with Mathieu van der Poel.…
