Christmas toy rush being driven by squishies and building sets
text:
Traditional games and stickers are helping to drive a bumper year for toy sales, figures show.

The data comes ahead of the crucial Christmas run-in for retailers, which peaks at 23 toys sold every second in the UK.

The number of toys sold up to October was 17% higher than the same period last year and growth is at a 10-year high, according to research company Circana.

The increase comes despite consumers' cost-of-living pressures, and there are signs that some of the biggest growth in sales is for toys priced between £5 and £10.

Despite relatively low sales in recent years, the toy sector has been buoyed by sales to "kidults".

The kidult market - which is toys and games for those aged over 12 - has been growing, particularly as adults buy toys for themselves.

This growth has continued with a 22% increase in the value of sales in the first half of the year.

But Melissa Symonds, UK toys director at Circana, said that toys for children - which still represents the majority of sales - had recorded a good year so far.

Growing public debate around children's screen time and the role of technology meant squishy toys, stickers and building sets such as Lego were popular.

"Connected toys account for less than 1% of market sales, showing that traditional, hands-on play remains overwhelmingly popular," she said.

Concerns have been raised about the suitability of some connected devices.

A BBC investigation found an AI teddy marketed as being "perfect" for children as young as three said "I can't help with killing you" after seemingly mishearing a question.

Meanwhile, debate has intensified about keeping youngsters free from smartphones during the school day .

One in five parents of children aged three to nine say the chance to play together as a family influences what they buy, according to market intelligence company The Insights Family.

Paul Reader, who chairs the Dream Toys selection panel of retailers and experts across the sector, said that parents wanted to engage with their children's play.

"Nothing beats a board game with that. Nothing beats a bit of interaction," he said.

The panel he chairs has selected a list of toys that retailers believe will be some of the most popular this year.

It includes variations on popular toys of recent years, including slime, a soft tiger that roars and grows, and a shark that breaks out of an egg.

Symonds said that, despite rising sales in the year so far, nearly half of toy sales came in the build-up to Christmas, and families were still looking closely at costs.

There was significant growth in toys priced between £5 and £10, she said.

Reader also urged anyone looking for a bargain to shop around, but to ensure that toys were bought from reputable traders so they were genuine and safe.

Are you going for traditional toys this Christmas? How much are you spending on toys this Christmas?

title: F1's divisive wet weather tyres to change in 2027 - what needs solving
author: Jon Noble
text:
Formula 1 tyre supplier Pirelli is close to finalising new specification wet-weather tyres for next season that already address concerns drivers voiced last weekend.

F1 had its first proper wet weekend of the year at Interlagos, with both qualifying and the race impacted by the rain.

Saturday’s running took place in conditions that were so extreme that the wet tyre, which has rarely been used in recent years, became the preferred choice for the conditions.

The race on Sunday was hit by showers, with drivers starting on intermediates, shifting to slicks and then reverting to inters towards the end when the rain returned.

But despite there being no major incidents – and the race being the first this year not interrupted by either a virtual or full safety car – drivers were still unhappy with how the wet rubber behaved.

Williams driver Carlos Sainz called for work to be done with Pirelli to deliver improvements in the future.

“The level of the wet and the inter is not good enough and we need to work with Pirelli on finding a better tyre,” he said.

“In the mixed conditions, the inter is still a very weak tyre at the rear, by the time it warms up the front is gone.

“And the extreme [wet], honestly, we had so much aquaplaning and a big lack of rear grip. So still missing a bit of development on these two tyres.”

The biggest challenge that drivers faced with the intermediate tyre on Sunday was getting them up to operating temperature.

This proved especially challenging on the low-speed laps to the grid, where a number of drivers were seen battling to keep their cars on the track.

And things weren't much better in the race, as Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson said it had been a real challenge to get the tyres into the right operating window.

The biggest problem was the temperature was much cooler,” Lawson said. “So even though there was less water on the laps of the grid, the cars were nearly undriveable. And the temps were just going down.

“We survived the start of the race, but at points when it rains a lot, it's not that the standing water is too much; it's that you can't actually keep the temperature in it. So, if we're on a track like Vegas and it rains, honestly, I think we're in trouble.”

But it was not just the fire-up that was a problem, as the inters proved very delicate in the race too.

Alex Albon, who described the laps to the grid as “insane”, said things were not much better once the tyres were up to temperature.

“It just feels like they never overheat or they never get up to temperature," he explained. "Then by the time you're circulating, the tread's already come off the tyre and then you're already struggling, you're sliding around.

“So you never feel good at any point in the race; it never feels like it comes alive.”

One of the common themes across this season is that the intermediate tyres feel worse than the previous version.

Alpine’s Pierre Gasly, who has long been sceptical about the inters ever since he tried them out at a wet test earlier this year, feels like they don't give as much confidence to push on as their predecessor.

“Generally, I must say they feel very poor,” he said. “The grip, I don't know if it's only with our car, but compared to the inters we used to have in the previous years, it just feels like they're nowhere. Extremely poor grip.

“The last stint felt [in Brazil] like I was driving on ice. So I want to review exactly what happened with our car. I don't know if it was the case for everyone, but it's genuinely not a very good tyre.”

Gasly's point is well-founded because Pirelli has had to design a tyre for the 2026 rules that is theoretically a step away from what is ideal.

The switch between straight mode and corner mode at the end of straights puts huge forces through the tyres, plus Pirelli needs to ensure its product can cope if active aero fails and cars are running down straights with maximum downforce.

So in a similar vein to how straight mode consequences have forced increases in minimum slick tyre pressures, Pirelli had to make a more robust intermediate tyre.

Furthermore, the minimum pressures have also gone up for wets and inters. In Brazil, for example, the minimum front pressures went up from 25.5psi last year on the inters to 28psi now, and on the wets from 22psi to 26.5psi.

The impact is a tyre that does not move around as much - which does not inspire confidence from the drivers to lean on and is also much harder to warm up.

The circumstances of the rule changes are something that Haas driver Ollie Bearman referenced in Brazil.

“They are definitely a bit worse than last year’s ones,” he said. “There’s a few more parameters that the manufacturer has to put in mind when they design these tyres, because of the straight mode, ride heights and things like that.

“The tyre feels a bit less forgiving: very stiff, very hard to warm up. Lap 1 was a big challenge. It’s a warm-up thing again for us, same as yesterday in quali.”

And while drivers did manage to get through the Brazilian weekend, Interlagos has a rough track surface and a twisty infield section that helps put temperature into the rubber. That may not be true at all venues on the calendar.

As Mercedes driver George Russell said: “I think it's important also to realise the three tracks driven on were very rough tarmacs and Malaysia was hot even in the rain.

“Singapore sprint race was still hot and [Brazil qualifying], even though it was raining, it was 30 degrees and the track was 30 degrees. Maybe in 15 degrees of Spa, we're giving different feedback.”

What Pirelli is looking to change

Pirelli always knew that it would need to fine-tune its wet tyres to the real 2026 cars, with the current designs having been based on feedback from mule car running last year.

It had planned a wet test in Bahrain in February to help it work on understanding things better using an artificially soaked track, but that had to be abandoned in the wake of the Iran war beginning.

Further wet weather tests over the season have been completed, which has put Pirelli on a path to introduce revised inters and wets for next season.

While Pirelli motorsport boss Dario Marrafuschi does not want to reveal too many specifics about what is coming for 2027, he has confirmed that the warm-up issues on the inter will be addressed.

“Tyre development is going ahead and we have a different spec for next year,” he told The Race.

"Some of the drivers were complaining about warm-up, so we have been working for next year on the warm-up phase, on the intermediates.”

He added: “It doesn't mean we are not satisfied with this year's specs because we had very good racing in Malaysia, in Singapore and in Brazil as well. But an optimisation can be done.

“We always listen quite openly to the comments of the drivers."

The final homologation of the wet and inter tyre designs with the FIA will be made in December, when more details will be revealed about what is changing for next year.

But Marrafuschi also believes there is an element that, in the meantime, teams will get a better handle on how to get more from the inter now that they have some proper experience of it.

He thinks what was highlighted in Brazil was how some squads and drivers seem to have had a better understanding of what was needed than others.

“Clearly there are some cars or drivers, some set-ups or whatever, that are more comfortable in one condition or the other," he explained.

“We saw in the beginning of the race, Lewis [Hamilton] having an astonishing performance, with zero warm-up problems at all.

"We know that other drivers, since the formation laps, were complaining about the front-end warm-up. So, there are some tunings that are in the hands of the teams.”

title: Tories would have to raise state pension age above 70 to keep triple lock, says minister
author: Heather Stewart
text:
Kemi Badenoch attacked reforms but is not being clear about how party would meet costs, Torsten Bell claims

Kemi Badenoch’s Conservatives would have to raise the state pension age above 70 to meet the cost of keeping the triple lock, Treasury minister Torsten Bell has claimed.

Labour has announced reforms to the triple-lock promise to come into force in the next parliament – with the initial proceeds earmarked for Andy Burnham’s national care service.

The Conservatives have attacked the move, and insisted they would stick with the triple lock, which increases the state pension each year in line with the largest of inflation, 2.5% or earnings growth.

However, Bell argued that with the costs of an unreformed triple lock increasing over time – to £50bn by 2050, according to government estimates – a Tory government would end up repeating the approach they took in the 2010s and speeding up planned increases to the state pension age.

“If you don’t want to have an adjustment to the triple lock, then you will need to do other things to make the state pension remotely sustainable,” he said. “We don’t need to guess what they would do because they’ve literally just done it, which is they repeatedly and at very short notice accelerated the increases in the state pension age.

“They did that in the in 2011 and in 2014. Some people had as little as five years’ notice.”

In 2013, the then chancellor, George Osborne, described increasing the pension age as, “one of the less controversial things we have done,” which had nevertheless delivered “absolutely enormous savings”.

The state pension age, now under review, is already expected to increase to 68 between 2044 and 2046; but Bell claimed the Conservatives would end up going further.

“All I’m saying is, Conservatives do raise the state pension age aggressively, and they have,” he said. “And even though they know that the triple lock should change, they are opposing it – and the consequence of that is they would end up making people wait into their 70s.”

The triple lock had previously been seen as too politically risky to reform, particularly in the light of the backlash against Labour’s plan to remove the winter fuel allowance from the vast majority of pensioners – which was subsequently abandoned .

But Bell said the public would prefer Burnham’s willingness to make an argument to what he claimed was the Conservatives’ failure to be honest.

“I think this is a bigger problem for Kemi Badenoch than she thinks. She thinks that her brand is principled, know what you think, tell it straight. And on this, she has done the opposite – we know that she knows it needs to change,” he said.

He cited the Conservative leader’s own suggestion, as recently as last year, that the triple lock should be means tested , and former Conservative chancellor Jeremy Hunt’s claim that the policy was an “anchor drag” on the public finances.

“The triple lock kind of is the final nail in the coffin of the idea that there’s anything fiscally responsible about modern Conservatism,” Bell said.

Under Labour’s planned reforms , the state pension will rise each year by the highest of inflation, or 2.5%. It will only rise in line with earnings growth if its value has slipped behind recent wage growth.

Bell, the MP for Swansea West since 2024, was previously director of the Resolution Foundation thinktank. He retained his role as pensions minister – working between the Treasury and the Department for Work and Pensions – when Burnham came to power in July.

He said the prime minister’s 10-year plan, which may now be delayed until the new year, will include a promise of a better deal for future pensioners. “It’s just really important to be able to say to people, ‘the comfortable retirement that your parents had: we’re going to make sure that today’s private sector workers have got those’,” he added.

title: Ukraine captures first Indonesian prisoner of war amid surge in Russian recruitment
author: Kate Lamb
text:
Capture of man from Java follows reports that hundreds are being recruited from the south-east Asian country as Moscow seeks to boost its war effort

Ukraine says it has captured its first Indonesian prisoner of war, amid what it says is a spike in recruitment by Russia from the south-east Asian nation.

The 49-year-old man from Java was taken to Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region to take part in a Russian assault, but managed to reach Ukrainian-held territory after the group came under drone attack, according to Ukraine’s state-run I Want to Live project. He was then captured by the Ukrainians.

According to the project, some 283 Indonesians were recruited in the first nine months of this year to fight for Russia against Ukraine. It said recruitment from Indonesia was no more than 10 in the previous three years.

The Russian embassy in Jakarta did not immediately respond to questions about the alleged recruitment effort but it is not the first time Russia has sought foreign mercenaries for its war effort.

In February, Kenya’s intelligence services reported that more than 1,000 Kenyans had been lured to fight for Russia.

A growing number of people from African countries – including Kenya, Uganda and South Africa – and elsewhere have been lured to the frontline as Russia seeks help to sustain its more than four-year war after invading Ukraine in February 2022.

This month Jakarta urged Moscow to ensure no Indonesians were drafted into its military, following the reported death in October of an Indonesian national serving with the military.

Indonesian foreign ministry spokesperson Yvonne Mewengkang said: “The Indonesian government asked the Russian government to take all necessary steps to ensure that no Indonesians will be recruited into the Russian military or any other military-related position in Russia through any avenues.”

Indonesia, she added, was particularly concerned about recruitment practices that could constitute human trafficking.

Days later, Indonesian police said they had identified a human trafficking syndicate targeting its nationals that used social media and messaging apps to recruit victims.

The posts promised lucrative jobs in logistics, border security and defence construction, but after the applicants travelled to Russia they were directed to sign contracts to serve as mercenaries, with some deployed to conflict zones, police said.

The ‘I Want to Live’ governmental initiative was established in September 2022 by the coordination headquarters for Prisoners of War with support from Ukraine defence ministry and defence intelligence (HUR).

It was designed to allow active-duty troops, including Russian servicemen and foreign nationals recruited into the Russian military, to safely surrender and exit the battlefield.

title: Robot vessels take on the dangerous work of mine hunting
text:
Traversing the Strait of Hormuz remains one of the most dangerous trips a vessel can take.

Despite assistance from the US Navy, ships are still being attacked .

"To transit the Strait of Hormuz you need agreement between the captain and the crew to take the risk. You need war risk insurance. And the captain has to make the final decision," says Steve Cameron, a former merchant navy officer and maritime consultant.

Missiles and drones are a threat from the air, but under the surface mines may also be lurking.

"If you're a captain, you'd like to see evidence mines aren't present," Cameron adds.

Modern mines rest on the seabed and detonate when they detect an acoustic or magnetic signal, triggering a pressure wave that will break the keel of a passing vessel.

Others can rise through shallow waters or float, or be powered towards a target.

The technology itself is not difficult or costly, but the mere threat can stop a tanker fleet from sailing.

Ian McFarlane of French defence group Thales is a naval architect who knows mine warfare well. "Mines are a very cheap way of waging a naval war, as the Royal Navy is acutely aware," he says.

Finding sea mines has traditionally been the job of specialist mine-hunting vessels, with crews of around 80 sailors.

To keep humans out of harm's way, an increasing amount of the work is done by systems that are autonomous and monitored from the shore.

They might only need 20 personnel, working in shifts on land. With the recruitment and retention challenges facing Nato navies these highly-portable robot systems are very attractive.

Such tech has been under development for 20 years.

During the 2003 Iraq war the US Navy poked around the seabed looking for mines with a torpedo-shaped robot called the Remus 100.

Pinging around with sonar these little machines operated down to around 100ft depth and spared divers a difficult and dangerous task.

The latest conflict in the Gulf is testing much more capable systems.

The US military is sparing with details about their mine-hunting craft, but we have seen glimpses of them.

Iranian forces hauled an uncrewed US autonomous sub , external out of the waters of the Strait of Hormuz in early September.

The Pentagon claimed this robot, an Extra Large Uncrewed Underwater Vehicle (XLUUV) from US autonomous defence tech venture Anduril, was a malfunctioning older device with no classified equipment on-board.

Whatever its mission, no sailors were imperilled. That, says William Lupton, a naval analyst with Shephard Group, "was a drop in the ocean compared to having prisoners taken", and part of the point of uncrewed vessels.

What if an uncrewed vessel is captured? Nato navies are reluctant to go into details, but computer drives can be wiped or destroyed remotely by various means. This may have taken place inside the humming circuit boards of the XLUUV seized by Iran.

Such autonomous tech is being embraced by forces around the world.

Cooperation between Thales, the Royal Navy, and France's Marine Nationale has produced a robot motor launch.

The Thales Uncrewed Surface Vehicle (USV) is packed with sensors programmed to detect mines via sonar that was developed for the oil and gas industries.

It tows a 5m long rectangular box, similar to a large torpedo, that takes a hi-resolution look at the seabed and creates a 3D picture refined by AI. The latest mines are designed to blend into their surroundings and the software spots anything that looks like a mine.

Autonomous systems are cheaper than conventional minehunters, plus they can be deployed, along with containerised control centres, by air.

Steve Prest, associate fellow at the RUSI defence think tank, introduced uncrewed mine hunting into the Royal Navy and was its first fleet robotics officer, a title he acquired in 2014.

"There is a bunch of ways to look for a mine using robot boats or robot subs, and while you can't prove the negative, that no mines are there, you can reduce the risk."

He says US robot minehunters can either blow up a mine or just mark the spot as somewhere to avoid.

"We'll see more use of autonomy but also the missions and capability will expand. And AI will be analysing data from those vessels on the spot as opposed to data being analysed when a drone returns."

The Royal Navy recently announced its concept of a hybrid navy - mixing drones with conventional warships. But Prest thinks for this vision to succeed the fleet must operate as one distributed force, sharing data in what he terms a cognitive architecture.

The robot only makes a real difference as part of this scheme and it's a mistake to focus on individual uncrewed assets. "Uncrewed or autonomous vessels are not the operating system. They are applications running on it."

While robots are on the rise, people are what really matter in the Strait.

Neil Roberts speaks for insurers at Lloyd's of London on marine matters and says the psychological impact of the mine threat is inescapable, as is the uncertainty around just how many mines, if any, are out there.

"The US says it has cleared the Omani route and believes the mine threat is being managed, with shipments running at about 75% of pre-conflict levels."

Fear of the unknown is the most potent aspect of the sea mine threat and robots are now the weapon of choice to confront that fear.
